questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Microstate and macrostate are different descriptions
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a microstate from the macrostate that contains it
questions.stem: One gas in a room is described in two ways at once: by which molecule sits in which state, and by the pressure and temperature read from a gauge. What is the relationship between those two descriptions?

options.text: The gauge reading summarises a huge number of microstates, and many microstates give the same reading
The gauge reading is one microstate among the many, and each microstate fixes a reading
options.misconception: treats a coarse summary as one of the detailed arrangements

options.text: The two descriptions are unrelated, since what a gauge shows has no bearing on the arrangements
options.misconception: believes a coarse description is independent of the arrangements

options.text: The two descriptions are equal in number, since each reading stands for one arrangement
options.misconception: believes the count of summaries equals the count of arrangements

questions.explanation: A macrostate is the coarse specification, and in a real gas it leaves an astronomical number of detailed arrangements unmentioned, all of which read the same on the gauge. That multiplicity is exactly what statistical mechanics counts when it assigns an entropy to the coarse description, and it is why two samples at the same pressure and temperature are treated as equivalent even though no two of their molecules are doing the same thing. The mapping runs one way only: the arrangement fixes the reading, but the reading fixes no arrangement at all.
questions.hint: Ask how many different arrangements could produce the same gauge reading.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a Boltzmann factor measures
questions.learningObjective: state the meaning and the temperature dependence of a Boltzmann factor
questions.stem: The fraction of particles in a state lying an energy E above the ground state is given by a Boltzmann factor involving E, the temperature and a constant. Which description is correct?

options.text: A high state is less populated than a low one by a factor that grows exponentially as the gap grows
A high state is more populated than a low one by a factor that grows exponentially as the gap grows
options.misconception: reverses the sign of the exponent in the factor

options.text: The populations of two states are equal whenever the temperature is high enough to excite them
options.misconception: believes a high temperature equalises all populations

options.text: The factor depends on the gap but not on the temperature, since energy alone sets the population
options.misconception: believes the populations are set by energy alone

questions.explanation: The factor is the exponential of a negative energy gap divided by a quantity proportional to temperature, so a bigger gap suppresses that state more, and a hotter sample suppresses it less. At a high temperature the distribution flattens towards equal populations, which is why hot matter excites many states at once, while at low temperature only the lowest states survive in force. The two directions of error here, reversing the sign of the exponent and dropping the temperature, are the most common ways to get populations backwards.
questions.hint: Think about whether raising the temperature fills higher states or empties them.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Entropy as a count of arrangements
questions.learningObjective: state the statistical definition of entropy
questions.stem: A sample can be in a very large number of arrangements, and the arrangements are not equally likely. Which statement describes the statistical definition of entropy?

options.text: Entropy is a constant times the logarithm of the number of arrangements consistent with the state
Entropy is that number of arrangements itself, so doubling it doubles the entropy linearly
options.misconception: believes entropy grows in direct proportion to the count

options.text: Entropy is the spread of the energies in the sample, independent of how many states exist
options.misconception: defines entropy as an energy spread rather than a count

options.text: Entropy is fixed by the total energy alone, since the arrangements do not affect it at all
options.misconception: believes the count of arrangements is irrelevant to entropy

questions.explanation: The definition is a constant, the Boltzmann constant, times the natural logarithm of the number of microstates inside a macrostate, and the logarithm is what makes the measure additive when independent pieces are put together. It is a logarithmic count, not a linear count, so doubling the number of arrangements adds a fixed small amount rather than doubling the entropy. The second law then says a spontaneous change proceeds toward arrangements that are more numerous, which is why a gas fills a room rather than concentrating in one corner.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of mathematical operation makes counts of arrangements add up cleanly.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a multiplicity enumerates
questions.learningObjective: state what a multiplicity counts and how it enters a probability
questions.stem: The multiplicity of a macrostate is the number of microstates it contains. How does that number enter a probability calculation?

options.text: A macrostate is as likely as the number of microstates it contains, out of the total available
Every macrostate is equally likely, so the count of microstates only affects the entropy
options.misconception: believes all macrostates are equally likely whatever their size

options.text: A macrostate is as likely as the logarithm of its microstate count, out of the total
options.misconception: puts the count inside the logarithm when computing a probability

options.text: The count of microstates cancels out, leaving a probability set by the macrostate label alone
options.misconception: believes the detailed arrangements do not affect likelihood

questions.explanation: When microstates are taken as equally likely, the chance of a macrostate is simply its share of the total count, so an outcome containing a million arrangements is a million times more likely than one containing a single arrangement. This is the whole engine of the subject: no hidden pull is needed, the overwhelming likelihood of what happens is a consequence of there simply being more ways to arrange things that way. The two standard errors are treating macrostates as equally likely and putting the count inside a logarithm when a probability is wanted.
questions.hint: Compare the count for one outcome with the count over all outcomes.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What temperature corresponds to statistically
questions.learningObjective: identify the statistical meaning of the temperature parameter
questions.stem: In the counting approach, the temperature appears as the parameter that decides how arrangements are weighted. What is that parameter doing?

options.text: It sets the exchange rate between energy and counting rate, so it fixes the balance of macrostates
It fixes the total energy of the sample, so every arrangement must have the same energy
options.misconception: believes a single temperature forces one energy on all states

options.text: It sets the volume available, so it is only a geometric quantity in disguise
options.misconception: identifies the temperature with the volume of the sample

options.text: It is a measure of the average speed of the particles, with no counting interpretation
options.misconception: reduces temperature to a mean speed and nothing more

questions.explanation: The temperature appears as the multiplier that trades energy against counting, which is why a low value makes arrangements expensive and a high value makes the distribution broad, and why the exchange rate is what sets the balance between the two macrostates a system can occupy. It does not fix the energy, since the states still have different energies and are traded against one another through that multiplier, and it is not a volume in disguise because it enters as a weight rather than as a constraint. A temperature of infinite value is the limit in which counting alone decides, and zero is the limit in which only the lowest arrangement survives.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the weighting of a high state when the parameter rises.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What equipartition does and does not cover
questions.learningObjective: state the equipartition result and its restriction to quadratic terms
questions.stem: Equipartition assigns an energy to each independent mode of a system in thermal contact. Which statement describes that result correctly?

options.text: Each quadratic term carries half a thermal energy, while a linear term does not share it
Every mode carries a whole thermal energy, whether its term is quadratic or linear
options.misconception: believes linear terms also get the half-share

options.text: Each mode carries half a thermal energy only at low temperature, and none at high
options.misconception: believes equipartition switches off above some temperature

options.text: Each mode carries half a thermal energy, so any frozen mode also keeps it at zero temperature
options.misconception: believes a frozen mode still holds a share of the energy

questions.explanation: The averaging that gives half a thermal energy to each quadratic term comes from an integral over a Gaussian, so a term that is linear or higher in the coordinate does not enjoy the same result, which is why a free particle's three velocity terms give the familiar three halves. The result also assumes the mode is actually being excited, so a mode frozen at very low temperature is not there to be counted, and a vibration that costs more than the thermal energy is frozen out. Both restrictions are why the classical law fails for solids at low temperature and for frozen vibrational modes in general.
questions.hint: Consider which mathematical form the averaging argument actually applies to.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Heat capacity as a count of degrees of freedom
questions.learningObjective: connect a gas heat capacity to its count of active degrees of freedom
questions.stem: A gas is heated at constant volume and its heat capacity is measured. Which statement correctly ties that number to the molecule?

options.text: The heat capacity counts the active quadratic modes per molecule, so a diatomic gas exceeds a monatomic one
The heat capacity counts the atoms per molecule, so a diatomic gas is twice a monatomic one
options.misconception: believes the atom count alone sets the heat capacity

options.text: The heat capacity is the same for both, since equipartition ignores whether a mode is rotational
options.misconception: believes every molecule carries the same heat capacity

options.text: The heat capacity counts the electrons, so a heavier molecule always absorbs less heat
options.misconception: believes the electron count sets the heat capacity

questions.explanation: At constant volume no work is done, so the heat supplied goes into raising the energy held in the active modes, and each active quadratic mode contributes half a thermal energy per molecule, which is why a diatomic gas with rotations as well as translations has the larger value. Freezing a mode out lowers that count, which is what happens to a vibrational mode at ordinary temperatures and to a rotation for some light molecules. The count is of modes, not of atoms or electrons, so a molecule with the same number of atoms but more accessible modes still absorbs more heat per kelvin.
questions.hint: Ask which modes are actually active at the temperature in question.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Heating a gas at constant volume
questions.learningObjective: explain why a fixed-volume heating needs less heat than a fixed-pressure one
questions.stem: A gas is heated through the same temperature rise in two ways: in a rigid sealed vessel, and in a cylinder under constant pressure. Which comparison is right?

options.text: The rigid vessel needs less heat, because at constant pressure the gas must also push the surroundings
The rigid vessel needs more heat, because a confined gas resists any change of state
options.misconception: believes confinement makes heating harder

options.text: Both need identical heat, since the temperature rise fixes the energy that must be supplied
options.misconception: believes a temperature rise alone fixes the heat needed

options.text: The constant-pressure case needs less heat, because expansion cools the gas as it occurs
options.misconception: claims expansion cools a gas being heated at constant pressure

questions.explanation: In the rigid vessel the boundary does not move, so the work term vanishes and all the heat supplied appears as added internal energy, while in the constant-pressure case the gas expands and does work on the surroundings, so the same temperature rise costs more heat. The two heat capacities therefore differ by the gas constant for each mole, and the difference is a direct measure of the expansion work. Neither vessel is resisting the temperature rise in any special way; the difference lies entirely in whether the boundary is allowed to move.
questions.hint: Look at the work term of the first law under each condition.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a solid's heat capacity falls at low temperature
questions.learningObjective: explain the low-temperature failure of the classical solid law
questions.stem: A solid's heat capacity is close to a fixed multiple of the gas constant over a wide range, but falls steeply at very low temperature. What accounts for the fall?

options.text: Fewer vibrational modes can be excited as the available thermal energy shrinks, so the count of modes drops
The bonds weaken at low temperature, so each mode carries less energy than the classical share
options.misconception: believes the bonds soften as the sample cools

options.text: The lattice expands on cooling, so the same heat is spread across more volume and appears smaller
options.misconception: confuses a change in volume with a change in heat capacity

options.text: The measured heat capacity falls only because the thermometer becomes less sensitive at low temperature
options.misconception: explains a real physical effect as an instrument artefact

questions.explanation: Each vibrational mode needs a finite amount of energy before it can carry any share at all, and as the thermal energy shrinks the modes with the largest spacing are switched off one by one, so the number of active modes falls and the heat capacity follows it down. The classical value of three shares per atom is therefore an upper limit reached only when the available energy is well above every vibrational spacing. This is one of the clearest places where the classical law fails and quantum counting is needed, and the failure is not an artefact of any thermometer.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen before a mode can carry its share of the energy.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Size of a flexible chain from its link count
questions.learningObjective: relate the size of a flexible chain to the number of links
questions.stem: A long flexible chain of identical links can point its links in many directions. How does the typical end-to-end distance grow with the number of links?

options.text: As the square root of the number of links, because random steps partially cancel one another
In direct proportion to the number of links, because each link adds its full length to the span
options.misconception: believes every link extends the span by its own length

options.text: As the number of links squared, since more steps multiply the possible distances together
options.misconception: believes the size grows with the square of the link count

options.text: Independently of the number of links, since bending makes the span independent of the length
options.misconception: believes folding leaves the end-to-end span fixed

questions.explanation: The links act as random steps whose transverse components largely cancel while the components along one axis add in root-mean-square fashion, so the typical span grows as the square root of the link count while the contour length grows in direct proportion. That gap between contour and span is the definition of a random walk and the reason such a material feels soft and rubbery. A fully extended chain would be as stiff as a rod, and the difference between the two regimes is what distinguishes an elastomer from a rigid plastic.
questions.hint: Compare the arithmetic sum of the links with the root-mean-square sum.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a correlation length measures in a chain
questions.learningObjective: state what a persistence length characterises
questions.stem: Real chains are not perfectly random: consecutive links tend to point in similar directions for a while, then wander off. What does the length over which that tendency survives measure?

options.text: The stiffness of the local direction, being the distance over which the direction is remembered
The total length of the molecule, since that is the longest distance the direction can persist
options.misconception: identifies the correlation length with the contour length

options.text: The spacing between links, which fixes how far a direction can be carried unchanged
options.misconception: confuses the link length with the memory length

options.text: The width of the molecule, being the largest offset at which directions still align
options.misconception: reads the correlation length as a transverse dimension

questions.explanation: The correlation length, usually quoted for a stiff chain such as a double helix or an aromatic backbone, is the distance over which the direction of one segment predicts the direction of the next, and it measures local stiffness rather than overall size. Short of that length the chain behaves like a stiff rod, and only over many multiples of it does the random-walk square-root behaviour take over. This is why a double helix with a correlation length of a few tens of nanometres behaves like a rod at short range yet contributes a long flexible tail to a polymer that contains it.
questions.hint: Ask what part of a long object the local direction can be trusted over.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a modulus reports about bonding
questions.learningObjective: interpret a measured elastic modulus in terms of bonding
questions.stem: Two samples are measured to have elastic moduli differing by a factor of a thousand. What does that factor say about their bonding?

options.text: The stiffer sample resists displacement far more per unit strain, so its bonds are much harder to stretch
The stiffer sample contains a thousand times more bonds, with each bond contributing equally
options.misconception: believes bond count alone accounts for the whole modulus

options.text: The stiffer sample has the same bonds but a thousand times fewer of them in the measured direction
options.misconception: reverses the effect of directional bond alignment

options.text: The stiffer sample has longer bonds, so each one needs more force before it yields
options.misconception: reads bond length rather than bond stiffness as the cause

questions.explanation: The modulus is the slope of the stress against strain, so it says how much force per unit area is needed to stretch the sample by a fixed fraction, and that is set by how steeply the interatomic potential rises under displacement. Strong directional bonds give a large modulus, layered or slip-prone bonding gives a small one, and a change in bonding type changes the modulus by orders of magnitude rather than by a few percent. Bond count matters too, which is why aligned fibres in a composite are stiffer along the fibre than across it, but the dominant difference here comes from the bonds themselves.
questions.hint: The modulus is a stress per unit strain, so ask what sets the size of that stress.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Distinguishing ductile from brittle behaviour
questions.learningObjective: distinguish ductile and brittle failure from the stress-strain record
questions.stem: Two specimens of the same shape are pulled in tension. One extends a long way before breaking and the other fractures almost immediately after yielding. What distinguishes them?

options.text: The first absorbs energy by deforming, while the second loses its load as a crack runs ahead
The first is stronger, since a longer extension means a larger force was needed throughout
options.misconception: believes extension measures the strength of a specimen

options.text: The second is harder, since a harder surface cannot deform before it fails
options.misconception: equates hardness with a resistance to cracking

options.text: The two differ only in surface finish, since cracks always start at the rougher face
options.misconception: attributes the difference entirely to surface finish

questions.explanation: A ductile specimen keeps absorbing work as it plastically deforms, and because a blunted crack tip resists further growth in that regime, the specimen warns you before it fails. A brittle one has no such warning: the crack sharpens as it runs, the load drops as it goes, and the stored energy is released all at once, so strength and toughness come apart. This is why design rules ban sharp notches and require a minimum toughness even in materials whose tensile strength looks adequate.
questions.hint: Ask which specimen can blunt a growing crack and which lets it accelerate.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What sets the current in a semiconductor
questions.learningObjective: identify the carriers that carry current in each doped semiconductor
questions.stem: A semiconductor conducts because charge carriers move through it. Which statement about those carriers is correct?

options.text: Doping type decides which carrier dominates, and the current is the product of density, charge and mobility
Doping type decides which carrier dominates, and the current depends only on the carrier density
options.misconception: believes mobility has no role in the current

options.text: The carrier is always an electron, since only electrons can move freely through a solid
options.misconception: believes only electrons carry current in a semiconductor

options.text: The carriers are the valence electrons of every atom, so the density cannot be raised by doping
options.misconception: believes doping cannot change the carrier population

questions.explanation: Adding a donor species leaves behind extra free electrons and adding an acceptor species leaves behind vacancies that behave as mobile positive charge, so the type of doping fixes which carrier carries most of the current. The conductivity is then the product of charge density and mobility, and both can be changed independently, which is why heavy doping raises the density while lowering the mobility through scattering. The gap between the two carrier populations is enormous in a doped sample, and it is that asymmetry rather than a new kind of particle that makes a junction work.
questions.hint: Write the current as carrier density times charge times velocity, and ask what sets the velocity.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a junction leaves a charge-free region
questions.learningObjective: explain the origin of the depletion region at a junction
questions.stem: Two differently doped pieces of semiconductor are joined, and a region near the join is left with almost no mobile carriers. What produced that region?

options.text: Carriers crossed the join and annihilated, leaving fixed ionised dopants behind to form a field
The dopants dissolved away at the join, so the region simply has nothing left to carry charge
options.misconception: invents a loss of dopant at the interface

options.text: The carriers are still there but frozen by the lattice, so they cannot respond to any field
options.misconception: confuses mobile carriers with bound charges

options.text: The region is a gap in the lattice where the crystal did not grow properly at the join
options.misconception: explains the region as a structural defect

questions.explanation: Before joining, carriers diffuse down their own concentration gradients, and the carriers that cross recombine with the ones already there, so the mobile population is swept out of a region near the interface. The dopant atoms cannot move, so they are left behind as fixed ions of both signs, and that fixed charge is what sustains the internal field which stops further diffusion. A reverse bias then widens the region, which is precisely why blocking voltage and capacitance both grow with the applied reverse bias.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two populations in the region can move away and which cannot.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Setting a detection threshold against false alarms
questions.learningObjective: explain how a threshold trades misses against false alarms
questions.stem: A detector reports a signal only when its reading crosses a chosen threshold. What happens as that threshold is raised?

options.text: False alarms fall while real signals are increasingly missed, and the two effects trade against each other
Both false alarms and missed signals fall, because a higher threshold is always a better choice
options.misconception: believes a higher threshold improves detection in every respect

options.text: False alarms rise while real signals are found more often, since the threshold amplifies weak signals
options.misconception: believes a threshold amplifies rather than discards

options.text: Neither changes, since the threshold only sets the units in which the reading is reported
options.misconception: believes a threshold cannot affect the outcome

questions.explanation: A threshold carves the noise distribution at a point, so raising it keeps more of the noise below the cut and fewer false alarms get through, but it also discards genuine signals that happen to fall low. The two rates are linked by the shape of the noise distribution, so there is no setting that improves both at once, only a choice of where on that curve to sit. The setting is usually made to meet a stated false-alarm rate, and the miss rate is then whatever that choice costs.
questions.hint: Consider where the threshold cuts into the spread of the noise readings.

questions.topic: Energy per quadratic degree of freedom
questions.learningObjective: compute the equipartition share for one quadratic mode
questions.stem: A mode in thermal contact with a reservoir at 300 K has an energy of the form one half a constant times the square of its coordinate. Using the Boltzmann constant 1.380649e-23 J/K, what is the mean energy of that mode, in joules?
questions.explanation: The equipartition share for a quadratic term is half the thermal energy, so the answer is one half of 1.380649e-23 multiplied by 300, that is 2.07e-21 J. The result is linear in the temperature, which is the signature of a mode that is genuinely being excited at the temperature in question. A whole thermal energy would double the answer, and that is the error made by counting a linear term as though it were quadratic.

questions.topic: Mean kinetic energy of one gas molecule
questions.learningObjective: compute the mean kinetic energy of a monatomic molecule
questions.stem: A monatomic ideal gas sits at 300 K. Using the Boltzmann constant 1.380649e-23 J/K, what is the mean kinetic energy of a single molecule, in joules? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: A molecule moving freely in three dimensions has three quadratic terms, so the mean kinetic energy is one and a half thermal energies, that is 1.380649e-23 times 300 times one and a half, which is 6.21e-21 J. Expressed in electronvolts the same value is about 0.039 eV, which is a useful reminder of how little energy a single molecule carries. Using a single share instead of one and a half would give the energy of a one-dimensional motion, which is not what a free molecule has.

questions.topic: Molar heat capacity of a solid
questions.learningObjective: compute the high-temperature molar heat capacity of a solid
questions.stem: A solid is warmed well above the range where its vibrational modes freeze out. Using the gas constant 8.314 J per mol K, what is the molar heat capacity predicted for it, in joules per mol K?
questions.explanation: Each atom contributes one vibrational mode with a kinetic and a potential quadratic term, so there are three shares per atom and the molar heat capacity is three times the gas constant, which is 24.9 J per mol K. The result is independent of which solid it is, which is a striking universality that holds only while the thermal energy exceeds every vibrational spacing. The value is close to that of many gases, which is why the two cannot be told apart from heat capacity alone at room temperature.

questions.topic: Heat capacity of a metal mass
questions.learningObjective: compute the heat capacity of a sample from its specific heat capacity
questions.stem: A sample of copper has a mass of 500 g and a specific heat capacity of 0.385 J per g K. What is the heat capacity of the whole sample, in joules per kelvin? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The heat capacity of a sample is its mass times its specific heat capacity, so 500 g multiplied by 0.385 J per g K is 192.5 J per K, and the units cancel to leave energy per kelvin as required. The specific heat capacity is a property of the material while the heat capacity is a property of this particular piece, and mixing the two up is a frequent source of an answer off by the mass. This value sits close to the classical prediction for a solid, three times the gas constant per mole, which for copper is about 24.4 J per mol K.

questions.stem: A sealed rigid vessel holds gas at a pressure of 1.0e5 Pa and a temperature of 300 K. It is heated to 450 K with the volume unchanged. What is the new pressure in pascals? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: With both the amount of gas and the volume fixed, the pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature, so the new pressure is 1.0e5 multiplied by 450 over 300, which is 1.5e5 Pa. A sealed vessel is the reason a car tyre or a pressure cooker becomes dangerous when heated, since the gas has nowhere to expand to.

questions.stem: A classical oscillator is in thermal contact with a reservoir at 300 K, so each of its two quadratic terms carries half a thermal energy. Using the Boltzmann constant 1.380649e-23 J/K, what is the mean total energy of the oscillator, in joules?
questions.explanation: The oscillator has one quadratic kinetic term and one quadratic potential term, so the total is two shares, that is one whole thermal energy, and 1.380649e-23 times 300 is 4.14e-21 J. A fixed barrier gives a current that grows in proportion to the exponential of the barrier against the thermal energy, so the doubling per interval is exactly the expected behaviour of a thermally activated process. questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: A stiffness claim that counting contradicts
questions.learningObjective: explain why a proposed explanation of a material property fails
questions.stem: A student claims that copper is stiffer than aluminium because copper conducts heat twice as well and better conduction must come with stiffer bonds. Explain in your own words why that reasoning does not hold.

answer.exemplar: The two properties are both consequences of the electron density and the bonding, but they respond to different parts of that description, so one does not predict the other. Thermal conduction depends on how readily electrons carry energy away from a hot region, which is governed by the mean free path and the density of mobile electrons, and metals with similar electron densities conduct at similar rates for unrelated reasons. Stiffness depends on the slope of the interatomic potential near its minimum, that is on how the bonds themselves resist being stretched, and the two metals differ there mainly because copper's atoms are closer together and its bonds are stiffer in a way that has nothing to do with how well it carries heat. Counting the arrangement of atoms and the shape of the potential is what fixes the modulus, and that count simply does not contain the conduction properties as an input. The honest test of the claim would be a pair of materials with similar conduction and very different stiffness, or similar stiffness and very different conduction, and such pairs are easy to find, which is what makes the inference untenable. What survives is a much weaker statement: both properties are set by the same electronic structure, so they can be correlated in a family of similar metals, and correlation is not the causal arrow the claim requires.

questions.explanation: Stiffness is fixed by the curvature of the interatomic potential while conduction is fixed by mobile-electron transport, and no counting of arrangements connects one to the other, so the correlation is not a cause.
questions.hint: Ask which microscopic quantity each of the two properties actually depends on.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why touching bodies reach one temperature
questions.learningObjective: explain the approach to thermal equilibrium statistically
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why two bodies in thermal contact end at one common temperature rather than settling at some intermediate fixed pair of temperatures.

answer.exemplar: Every exchange of energy between the two bodies moves one arrangement into another, and the number of arrangements available to a body at a given energy grows as the exponential of that energy divided by the thermal energy, so a body sitting above the common temperature has vastly more of its own arrangements than one below it. The chance of a transfer from the hot body to the cold one is therefore much greater than the chance of the reverse transfer, and that imbalance persists for as long as any temperature difference remains. The difference does not merely average away, it is driven towards zero, because the flow continues in the biased direction until the populations of exchangeable arrangements match. At that point the exchange still happens in both directions at equal rates, so energy moves back and forth continuously while the readings stay constant, and that is equilibrium rather than a cessation of motion. The common temperature is fixed by the total energy shared between the two bodies and their joint count of arrangements, which is why it need not equal either starting temperature and can lie quite close to the cooler body when its heat capacity is much larger.

questions.explanation: The population of exchangeable arrangements grows exponentially with energy, so energy flows from the body with more of them until the two counts match, and equality of the two flow rates at that point is what equilibrium means.
questions.hint: Compare the number of arrangements available to the hotter and cooler body.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why the loss in a fibre depends on wavelength
questions.learningObjective: explain why transmission losses in a fibre are not the same at every wavelength
questions.stem: A fibre carries short wavelengths much further than long ones, and also carries very long ones badly. Explain in your own words why the loss is not flat across the spectrum.

answer.exemplar: Two different mechanisms dominate at opposite ends of the spectrum, which is what produces the characteristic dip in the middle. At short wavelengths the loss comes from scattering by tiny imperfections in the glass, and the scattered amount grows steeply as the wavelength gets shorter, roughly as the inverse fourth power of the wavelength, so light a tenth as long is scattered ten thousand times more strongly. At long wavelengths the loss is absorption, since the glass and the impurities absorb particular bands of the infrared, and beyond those bands the material begins to absorb strongly again. Between the two regions lies a window in which neither mechanism is strong, and that window is where the best fibres are engineered to operate. Working away from it costs range immediately: moving to a shorter wavelength for a higher data rate runs straight into the steep scattering wall, which is why a well chosen operating point beats simply choosing the shortest wavelength available. The minimum in the loss curve is therefore a compromise between two competing mechanisms, not a property of a single one.

questions.explanation: Short wavelengths are lost steeply to scattering on imperfections while long ones are absorbed in particular bands, so the best transmission lies in the window between the two mechanisms rather than at either end.
questions.hint: Identify which mechanism takes over at each end of the wavelength range.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Separating the two kinds of measurement error
questions.learningObjective: explain the split between random and systematic error and the role of calibration
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why repeating a measurement many times and calibrating an instrument against a reference are solving two different problems.

answer.exemplar: Repeating a measurement attacks the part of the error that changes from one attempt to the next, so the scatter of the repeats falls as the square root of how many were made, and the mean of the repeats becomes a better estimate of the true value. That works because those errors have no preferred sign and cancel in the average. A systematic error does not behave that way: an offset in the zero, a gain that is a few percent low, a probe that reads high because of the sample in front of it, all of them push every repeat in the same direction, so averaging them leaves them untouched and may make them look smaller and better behaved than they are. Calibration is what addresses that second class, by comparing the instrument with something whose value is already known, and it produces a correction that is then applied to every future reading. The two are complementary rather than alternatives, and a careful result quotes both: the scatter of the repeats for the random part and the size of the correction, with its own uncertainty, for the systematic part. Reporting only the scatter of a set of repeats, with no calibration, overstates the precision of the answer.

questions.explanation: Repetition shrinks the error that varies from attempt to attempt, and only that error, while a fixed offset or gain survives repetition and must be measured against a known reference and subtracted.
questions.hint: Ask which class of error changes sign between repeats and which does not.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why coherent emission needs more particles in the upper state
questions.learningObjective: explain the requirement of a population inversion for laser action
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why a two-level system on its own cannot amplify light, and what has to be arranged to make amplification possible.

answer.exemplar: In thermal equilibrium the populations of the two levels follow the Boltzmann factor, so the upper level is always the less populated, and absorption therefore always wins over stimulated emission by exactly the population ratio. Since absorption removes a photon from the field and stimulated emission adds one with the same energy, phase and direction, the net effect of a beam passing through is a loss, and no amount of intensity can reverse a ratio fixed by counting. The way out is to arrange for the upper level to be more populated than the lower one, which requires pumping from a third level or a fourth level scheme, because a pump can feed the upper state faster than it empties while the lower state is emptied rapidly by a non-radiative route. Once the inversion is there, a photon travelling through stimulates emission from more than one upper-state particle than the number of absorbing lower-state particles, and the field grows. This is why the effect has a threshold and why the emitted light is coherent, since every stimulated event copies the phase and direction of the stimulating photon, unlike spontaneous emission which radiates in all directions at random.

questions.explanation: With a Boltzmann population the absorption always exceeds the stimulated emission, so the net effect on a beam is a loss, and amplification requires an inversion that a pump through extra levels can sustain.
questions.hint: Compare the two rates that remove and add photons from the same field.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: How a ductile material survives a notch
questions.learningObjective: explain why ductility protects a specimen from a stress raiser
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why a notch is far less dangerous in a material that deforms plastically than in one that does not.

answer.exemplar: A notch concentrates stress, and the severity of that concentration grows with the square root of the notch size, so a small defect multiplies the local stress well beyond the nominal value. In a brittle material the crack that initiates at the notch tip simply continues, because the tip stays sharp, and the loading it carries is released all at once when it runs. In a ductile material the material around the tip yields and flows, which does two things at once: it spreads the deformation over a region rather than concentrating it at one point, and it blunts the tip by rounding it off. A blunted tip has a much lower concentration factor for the same applied stress, so the crack advances in small stable steps and the specimen absorbs work the whole time, which is why ductile components give warning through measurable permanent deformation before failing. This is the quantitative reason design codes forbid sharp corners and notches, and why a specified toughness has to be checked even when the nominal stress looks modest. It is also why two specimens of the same strength can have very different behaviour when one is notched and the other is not.

questions.explanation: Plastic flow at a notch tip blunts the crack and spreads the deformation, which lowers the local stress intensity and lets the crack advance in stable steps instead of running away.
questions.hint: Ask what the material does at the crack tip while the load is applied.

The correlation structure comes next, since treating correlated inputs as independent is the commonest way to produce an overconfident budget, and only then can the systematic effects be removed and any residual offset quoted on its own. The propagation is the final step, and it is the one that must come last because it consumes everything established before it, with the random contributions added in quadrature and the systematic ones carried as a separate line.

The fracture surface is examined for beach marks and the origin of the crack is located
The failed component is kept intact and the surrounding parts are left undisturbed

questions.explanation: The first thing to do is nothing destructive, since a fatigue surface carries the record of its own history and cleaning, cutting or polishing it can erase the evidence before anyone has read it. The surface is then examined for the beach marks left by each cycle and the origin found, usually at a notch, a hole or a change of section, and that origin is what tells you which local stress to reconstruct. Checking the material against the specification comes next, because a wrong hardness or an undetected flaw changes which stress the comparison should use. Only then is the loading history rebuilt and compared with the fatigue data, which is what separates a design fault from a material fault.
questions.hint: Preservation has to come before anything that could damage the evidence.
